source_org: E. H. Weber; G. T. Fechner
author: E. H. Weber; G. T. Fechner
title: Weber's law / Weber–Fechner law
statement: The smallest noticeable difference in a stimulus (size, brightness, weight) is a constant proportion of the original stimulus, so perceived intensity grows roughly with the logarithm of physical intensity.
rationale: Differences in size, weight, color or spacing that are meant to signal hierarchy must be proportionally large enough to be noticed; tiny increments between heading levels or states read as identical.
audit_check: Are differences between hierarchy levels and states (heading sizes, active vs inactive, selected vs unselected) large enough to be noticed at a glance?
threshold: JND is a constant ratio (e.g., ~2% for brightness in lab conditions); use clearly distinct steps such as a type scale ratio of 1.2 or more.
citation: Fechner, G. T. (1860). Elemente der Psychophysik. Precursor to the 1900–present period, still foundational.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. S. Stevens
title: Stevens' power law
statement: Perceived magnitude grows as a power function of physical magnitude, with a different exponent per sense; perceived area grows more slowly than actual area.
rationale: Area-based encodings (bubble charts, icon sizes) are systematically underestimated; prefer length/position encodings for quantitative comparison.
audit_check: Do charts encode quantities with position or length rather than area or volume when accurate comparison matters?
threshold: Exponent ~0.7 for area, ~1.0 for length, ~3.5 for electric shock.
citation: Stevens, S. S. (1957). On the psychophysical law. Psychological Review, 64(3), 153–181.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: M. Wertheimer; K. Koffka; W. Köhler
author: M. Wertheimer; K. Koffka; W. Köhler
title: Law of Prägnanz (simplicity / good figure)
statement: People perceive ambiguous or complex images in the simplest form possible, because that interpretation needs the least cognitive effort.
rationale: Simple, regular shapes and layouts are processed faster; visually complex compositions get mentally simplified, sometimes wrongly.
audit_check: Can the layout be understood as a few simple groups and shapes, or does it require effort to parse?
citation: Wertheimer, M. (1923). Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt II. Psychologische Forschung, 4, 301–350; Koffka, K. (1935). Principles of Gestalt Psychology.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Wertheimer
title: Law of proximity
statement: Objects that are near each other are perceived as a group.
rationale: Spacing is the primary tool for grouping: labels must be closer to their own field than to neighbouring fields; related controls should sit together and unrelated ones apart.
audit_check: Is each label, caption and helper text closer to the element it describes than to any other element? Is spacing between groups larger than spacing within groups?
threshold: Inter-group spacing should be noticeably larger than intra-group spacing (commonly ≥ 2×).
citation: Wertheimer (1923), Psychologische Forschung 4.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Wertheimer
title: Law of similarity
statement: Elements that share visual characteristics (color, shape, size, orientation) are perceived as related or as having the same function.
rationale: Things that look the same must behave the same; links, buttons and interactive states need consistent styling, and non-interactive elements must not mimic interactive styling.
audit_check: Do all elements with the same function share the same visual treatment, and do elements with different functions look different?
citation: Wertheimer (1923).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Gestalt psychologists
title: Law of closure
statement: People mentally complete incomplete shapes and perceive a whole even when parts are missing.
rationale: Icons and logos can be minimal; also explains why partially visible content (a cut-off card) signals that more content can be scrolled.
audit_check: Where horizontal scrolling or more content exists, is part of the next item visible to signal continuation?
citation: Koffka (1935). Principles of Gestalt Psychology.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Wertheimer
title: Law of continuity (good continuation)
statement: Elements arranged on a line or curve are perceived as more related than elements not on the line.
rationale: Align items on clear axes; carousels, timelines, and step indicators rely on continuity to show sequence.
audit_check: Are related items aligned along a common axis so the eye follows them in order?
citation: Wertheimer (1923).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Wertheimer
title: Law of common fate
statement: Elements that move together in the same direction are perceived as a group.
rationale: Animate related elements together; elements that move independently are read as separate.
audit_check: When items animate, do grouped items move together and unrelated items move separately?
citation: Wertheimer (1923).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Rubin
title: Figure–ground
statement: People instinctively separate a visual field into a figure (foreground object) and ground (background).
rationale: Modals, menus and popovers need clear separation (scrim, shadow, contrast) from the background; low contrast between figure and ground causes ambiguity.
audit_check: Are overlays, dialogs and cards clearly separated from the background (scrim, elevation, border or contrast)?
citation: Rubin, E. (1915). Synsoplevede Figurer.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Gestalt psychologists
title: Law of symmetry and order
statement: Symmetrical elements are perceived as belonging together and as a stable, coherent whole.
rationale: Symmetric compositions feel orderly and calm; asymmetry can be used deliberately to draw attention.
audit_check: Is symmetry or deliberate asymmetry used purposefully rather than accidentally?
citation: Koffka (1935).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. E. Palmer
title: Law of common region
statement: Elements located within the same bounded area (a box, card or background) are perceived as a group, even overriding proximity.
rationale: Cards, panels, and shaded sections are strong grouping tools; misplaced borders create false groups.
audit_check: Do containers (cards, panels, backgrounds) enclose exactly the elements that belong together?
citation: Palmer, S. E. (1992). Common region: A new principle of perceptual grouping. Cognitive Psychology, 24(3), 436–447.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. E. Palmer & I. Rock
title: Law of uniform connectedness
statement: Elements that are visually connected (by lines, arrows or shared color regions) are perceived as more related than elements without a connection.
rationale: Connectors in steppers, flow diagrams and timelines strongly communicate relationship and sequence.
audit_check: Are relationships that matter (steps, hierarchy, links between items) shown with visual connectors where appropriate?
citation: Palmer, S. & Rock, I. (1994). Rethinking perceptual organization: The role of uniform connectedness. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 1(1), 29–55.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. von Restorff
title: Von Restorff effect (isolation effect)
statement: When multiple similar items are present, the one that differs from the rest is most likely to be noticed and remembered.
rationale: Make the primary action or key information visually distinct; but if many things are emphasized, nothing stands out. Do not rely on color alone to make the difference.
audit_check: Is there exactly one visually dominant primary action per view, distinct from secondary actions by more than color alone?
citation: von Restorff, H. (1933). Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld. Psychologische Forschung, 18, 299–342.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Treisman & G. Gelade
title: Preattentive processing / feature integration theory
statement: Some visual features (color hue, size, orientation, motion, enclosure) are detected in parallel in under ~250 ms without focused attention; conjunctions of features require slower serial search.
rationale: Use a single distinctive preattentive feature to make critical items (errors, alerts, selected state) pop out; combinations of features do not pop out.
audit_check: Can critical status (errors, alerts, selection) be spotted within a glance because it differs in one strong visual feature?
citation: Treisman, A. & Gelade, G. (1980). A feature-integration theory of attention. Cognitive Psychology, 12(1), 97–136.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: A. Mack & I. Rock; D. Simons & C. Chabris
author: A. Mack & I. Rock; D. Simons & C. Chabris
title: Inattentional blindness
statement: People engaged in a task often fail to notice unexpected, clearly visible objects outside their focus of attention.
rationale: Messages placed away from where the user is working (e.g., a status message in a corner while the user is typing in a form) are frequently missed; place feedback at the locus of attention.
audit_check: Is feedback shown where the user is looking (next to the triggering control) rather than in a distant region?
citation: Simons, D. J. & Chabris, C. F. (1999). Gorillas in our midst. Perception, 28(9), 1059–1074; Mack & Rock (1998). Inattentional Blindness. MIT Press.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: R. Rensink, J. K. O'Regan & J. Clark
author: R. Rensink, J. K. O'Regan & J. Clark
title: Change blindness
statement: People often fail to notice large changes to a scene when the change coincides with a visual disruption such as a page reload, flicker or scroll.
rationale: Content that changes after a reload or during a transition (prices, cart counts, validation messages) may go unnoticed; animate or highlight changes and announce them to assistive technology.
audit_check: When content updates (cart count, totals, inline messages), is the change made noticeable (highlight, motion, focus or live region)?
citation: Rensink, R. A., O'Regan, J. K., & Clark, J. J. (1997). To see or not to see: The need for attention to perceive changes in scenes. Psychological Science, 8(5), 368–373.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: J. P. Benway & D. M. Lane
author: J. P. Benway & D. M. Lane
title: Banner blindness
statement: Users tend to ignore page elements that look like advertisements or that sit in locations where ads usually appear, even when they contain useful information.
rationale: Do not style important content or calls to action like ads (boxed, animated, flashy, in right rail or top banner positions).
audit_check: Is any important information or CTA styled or positioned in a way that resembles advertising?
citation: Benway, J. P. & Lane, D. M. (1998). Banner blindness: Web searchers often miss "obvious" links. Internetworking, ITG Newsletter.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Nielsen; K. Pernice (NN/g)
title: F-shaped scanning pattern (and other scanning patterns)
statement: Eye-tracking shows that on text-heavy pages without strong formatting, users scan in an F-shape: across the top, then a shorter horizontal sweep, then down the left side. Other patterns include layer-cake (scanning headings), spotted, marking and commitment patterns.
rationale: Front-load headings, links and bullet points with the most informative words; use clear subheadings so users can layer-cake scan instead of F-scan.
audit_check: Do headings, list items and link texts start with the information-carrying words? Is text broken up with descriptive subheadings?
citation: Nielsen, J. (2006). F-Shaped Pattern for Reading Web Content. NN/g; Pernice, K. (2017). F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant. NN/g.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Attributed to E. Arnold
title: Gutenberg diagram (reading gravity)
statement: For evenly distributed, text-heavy layouts in left-to-right languages, the eye tends to move from the top-left (primary optical area) to the bottom-right (terminal area), with weaker attention to the other two quadrants.
rationale: Place the final call to action where the reading path ends; mirror for right-to-left languages. Weaker than F-pattern evidence; treat as heuristic.
audit_check: In dense layouts, does the primary action sit where the reading path naturally terminates?
citation: Attributed to Edmund C. Arnold, newspaper design (mid-20th century).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. C. Cherry; D. Broadbent
title: Selective attention / cocktail party effect
statement: People can focus on one stream of information while filtering others, but salient, personally relevant signals (such as one’s own name) break through the filter.
rationale: Personalised or highly salient cues capture attention; use them sparingly for important events, not for marketing noise.
audit_check: Are attention-grabbing cues (name, sound, motion, badges) reserved for events that genuinely need attention?
citation: Cherry, E. C. (1953). Some experiments on the recognition of speech, with one and with two ears. JASA, 25(5), 975–979; Broadbent, D. (1958). Perception and Communication.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: C. D. Wickens
title: Multiple resource theory
statement: People have separate pools of attentional resources (visual vs auditory, spatial vs verbal, perception vs response); tasks that compete for the same resource interfere more than tasks using different resources.
rationale: In multitasking contexts (driving, monitoring, voice + screen), distribute information across modalities; avoid asking users to read while also reading.
audit_check: In contexts where the user is busy (driving, cooking, operating equipment), is information delivered through a modality that is not already occupied?
citation: Wickens, C. D. (2002). Multiple resources and performance prediction. Theoretical Issues in Ergonomics Science, 3(2), 159–177.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. R. Endsley
title: Situation awareness (3 levels)
statement: Situation awareness has three levels: perception of elements in the environment, comprehension of their meaning, and projection of their future status.
rationale: Dashboards and monitoring tools should support all three levels: show current state, explain what it means, and indicate trends or predictions.
audit_check: Does the dashboard or status view show what is happening, what it means, and what is likely to happen next?
citation: Endsley, M. R. (1995). Toward a theory of situation awareness in dynamic systems. Human Factors, 37(1), 32–64.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: G. A. Miller
title: Miller's law (7 ± 2)
statement: The span of immediate memory is limited to roughly seven (plus or minus two) chunks of information; later research (Cowan 2001) suggests closer to four chunks.
rationale: Do not require users to hold many items in memory across steps; chunk information (phone numbers, codes) and keep critical information visible. Do NOT misuse it to cap menu lengths: menus are recognized, not memorized.
audit_check: Does any step require remembering information shown on a previous screen? Are long codes and numbers chunked?
citation: Miller, G. A. (1956). The magical number seven, plus or minus two. Psychological Review, 63(2), 81–97.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: N. Cowan
title: Working memory capacity of ~4 chunks
statement: When rehearsal and chunking are prevented, adults hold about 3–5 meaningful chunks in working memory.
rationale: Design for a working memory limit of around four items: comparisons, multi-step instructions, and options to remember should be kept small or kept on screen.
audit_check: Does any task require comparing or remembering more than ~4 items without them being visible together?
citation: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: G. A. Miller; W. Chase & H. Simon
author: G. A. Miller; W. Chase & H. Simon
title: Chunking
statement: Grouping individual pieces of information into larger meaningful units increases how much can be held and processed.
rationale: Format long numbers and codes in groups (e.g., 4-4-4-4 for card numbers), split long forms into logical sections, and group content under headings.
audit_check: Are long strings (card numbers, IBANs, phone numbers, codes) displayed and accepted in chunked format? Are long forms and pages divided into labeled groups?
citation: Chase, W. G. & Simon, H. A. (1973). Perception in chess. Cognitive Psychology, 4(1), 55–81.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Baddeley & G. Hitch
title: Working memory model
statement: Working memory consists of a central executive, a phonological loop (verbal), a visuospatial sketchpad and (added 2000) an episodic buffer, each with limited capacity.
rationale: Verbal and visual information can be processed partly in parallel; overloading one channel (e.g., long spoken instructions in voice UIs) quickly exceeds capacity.
audit_check: In voice and audio interfaces, are spoken lists and instructions short enough to be held in the phonological loop (about 3–5 items)?
citation: Baddeley, A. D. & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. Psychology of Learning and Motivation, 8, 47–89.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Sweller
title: Cognitive load theory
statement: Learning and task performance suffer when total cognitive load exceeds working memory capacity. Load is intrinsic (task complexity), extraneous (caused by poor presentation) and germane (useful effort).
rationale: Remove extraneous load: unnecessary decoration, split attention between distant related items, redundant text, unclear navigation.
audit_check: Is there content, decoration or interaction that adds effort without helping the user complete their task?
citation: Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257–285.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: P. Chandler & J. Sweller
title: Split-attention effect
statement: When people must mentally integrate information from separate sources (a diagram and its distant legend), cognitive load rises and performance drops.
rationale: Put labels directly on charts, place help text beside the field it explains, and keep error messages next to the input in error.
audit_check: Are legends, help texts and error messages placed adjacent to the items they refer to?
citation: Chandler, P. & Sweller, J. (1991). Cognitive load theory and the format of instruction. Cognition and Instruction, 8(4), 293–332.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Memory research (e.g., Shepard 1967; Standing 1973)
title: Recognition is easier than recall
statement: People are far better at recognizing previously seen information than at recalling it unaided; recognition memory for pictures is extremely large.
rationale: Show options, recent items, examples and visible menus instead of requiring users to remember commands, codes or prior answers.
audit_check: Can users choose from visible options (menus, suggestions, recent items) rather than having to remember and type values?
citation: Shepard, R. N. (1967). Recognition memory for words, sentences, and pictures. JVLVB, 6(1), 156–163; Standing, L. (1973). Learning 10,000 pictures. QJEP, 25(2), 207–222.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Paivio
title: Picture superiority effect / dual coding
statement: Information presented as pictures (or pictures plus words) is remembered better than words alone, because it is encoded both verbally and visually.
rationale: Pair icons with text labels; use illustrations for key concepts. Icons alone are often ambiguous, but icon + label beats either alone.
audit_check: Are icons accompanied by visible text labels, especially for less common actions?
citation: Paivio, A. (1971). Imagery and Verbal Processes. Holt, Rinehart & Winston.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. Ebbinghaus; B. Murdock
title: Serial position effect (primacy & recency)
statement: Items at the beginning (primacy) and end (recency) of a list are remembered best; middle items are most easily forgotten.
rationale: Place the most important navigation items and options first and last; avoid burying key items in the middle of long lists.
audit_check: Are the most important items placed at the start or end of navigation bars and lists?
citation: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482–488.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: B. Zeigarnik
title: Zeigarnik effect
statement: People remember uncompleted or interrupted tasks better than completed ones.
rationale: Progress indicators and incomplete-profile prompts motivate completion; ethically, do not weaponize open loops (endless badges, artificial incompleteness).
audit_check: Do multi-step tasks show progress and remaining steps, and is "unfinished" status used honestly?
citation: Zeigarnik, B. (1927). Das Behalten erledigter und unerledigter Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 9, 1–85.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Ovsiankina
title: Ovsiankina effect
statement: People feel a tendency to resume an interrupted task.
rationale: Let users save progress and resume where they left off; show a clear "continue where you left off" entry point.
audit_check: Can users leave a long task and resume it later without losing work, and is the resume path obvious?
citation: Ovsiankina, M. (1928). Die Wiederaufnahme unterbrochener Handlungen. Psychologische Forschung, 11, 302–379.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. Ebbinghaus
title: Forgetting curve & spacing effect
statement: Memory for new information decays rapidly without reinforcement; spaced repetition slows forgetting.
rationale: Do not assume users remember onboarding tips or settings explained once; surface guidance contextually at the moment of need.
audit_check: Is guidance available in context when needed, rather than only in a one-time onboarding tour?
citation: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis. Precursor to the 1900–present period.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: K. Craik; P. Johnson-Laird; D. Norman
author: K. Craik; P. Johnson-Laird; D. Norman
title: Mental models
statement: People form internal, simplified models of how a system works and use them to predict behavior; mismatches between the user’s model and the system’s model cause errors.
rationale: Match the system image to users’ existing models (real-world metaphors, conventions); reveal how things work through feedback and clear structure.
audit_check: Does the interface behave the way a first-time user would predict? Where it does not, is the actual behavior explained?
citation: Craik, K. (1943). The Nature of Explanation; Norman, D. A. (1983). Some observations on mental models. In Gentner & Stevens (Eds.), Mental Models.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: P. Pirolli & S. Card
title: Information foraging theory & information scent
statement: People seeking information behave like animals foraging for food: they follow cues (information scent) and leave a patch when the expected gain drops below the cost of moving on.
rationale: Links, labels and navigation must carry strong scent: specific, predictable words that tell users what they will find. Weak scent (vague labels like "Solutions", "Learn more") causes pogo-sticking and abandonment.
audit_check: Do navigation labels and link texts clearly predict the content behind them? Would a user know which link to choose for their goal?
citation: Pirolli, P. & Card, S. (1999). Information foraging. Psychological Review, 106(4), 643–675.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: H. A. Simon
title: Satisficing
statement: People choose the first option that seems good enough rather than searching for the optimal one.
rationale: Users click the first plausible link instead of reading all options (Krug 2000); make the right choice the most obviously plausible one.
audit_check: Would a user scanning quickly pick the correct option first, or is a plausible-but-wrong option more prominent?
citation: Simon, H. A. (1956). Rational choice and the structure of the environment. Psychological Review, 63(2), 129–138.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: N. Slamecka & P. Graf
title: Generation effect
statement: Information people generate themselves is remembered better than information they only read.
rationale: For learning products, let users actively produce answers; for task tools, do not make users generate information the system already knows.
audit_check: Does the product ask users to produce information it could pre-fill (bad), or ask learners to recall information to reinforce it (good, in learning contexts)?
citation: Slamecka, N. J. & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect. JEP: Human Learning and Memory, 4(6), 592–604.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: P. M. Fitts
title: Fitts's law
statement: The time to move to a target is a function of the distance to and the size of the target: MT = a + b·log2(2D/W) (Shannon formulation: MT = a + b·log2(D/W + 1)).
rationale: Make frequent and important targets large and close to where the pointer or thumb already is; use screen edges and corners (effectively infinite targets on desktop); keep destructive actions away from common ones.
audit_check: Are primary actions large and close to the user’s current focus? Are small targets avoided for frequent actions? Are destructive actions not adjacent to frequent actions?
threshold: MT = a + b·log2(D/W + 1); see also WCAG 2.5.8 (24×24 CSS px min) and 2.5.5 (44×44).
citation: Fitts, P. M. (1954). The information capacity of the human motor system in controlling the amplitude of movement. JEP, 47(6), 381–391; MacKenzie, I. S. (1992). Fitts' law as a research and design tool in HCI. HCI, 7(1), 91–139.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: W. E. Hick; R. Hyman
title: Hick–Hyman law
statement: Decision time increases logarithmically with the number and (equally likely) complexity of choices: RT = a + b·log2(n + 1).
rationale: Reduce the number of simultaneous choices for time-critical or novice decisions; highlight recommended options; break complex choices into steps. Does not apply well to searching unfamiliar lists, which is linear.
audit_check: At key decision points (pricing, onboarding, main navigation), is the number of options minimized and is a recommended choice indicated?
citation: Hick, W. E. (1952). On the rate of gain of information. QJEP, 4(1), 11–26; Hyman, R. (1953). Stimulus information as a determinant of reaction time. JEP, 45(3), 188–196.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Accot & S. Zhai
title: Steering law
statement: The time to move a pointer through a tunnel (such as a cascading menu path) is proportional to the tunnel’s length divided by its width.
rationale: Long, narrow hover paths (nested flyout menus) are slow and error-prone; widen paths, add hover-intent delays/triangles, or avoid deep cascades.
audit_check: Do nested menus require the user to steer through narrow paths without closing accidentally?
threshold: T = a + b·(A/W) for straight tunnels
citation: Accot, J. & Zhai, S. (1997). Beyond Fitts' law: Models for trajectory-based HCI tasks. CHI '97, 295–302.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Card, T. Moran & A. Newell
author: S. Card, T. Moran & A. Newell
title: Keystroke-Level Model (KLM)
statement: Expert, error-free task time can be predicted by summing standard operator times: K (keystroke), P (point), B (button press), H (home hands), M (mental preparation), R (system response).
rationale: Use KLM to compare design alternatives for efficiency (e.g., number of field switches, pointing vs keyboard).
audit_check: For frequent expert tasks, has the number of operators (clicks, field switches, mental decisions) been minimized?
threshold: K ≈ 0.2 s (avg skilled typist; 0.08–1.2 s range), P ≈ 1.1 s, B ≈ 0.1 s, H ≈ 0.4 s, M ≈ 1.35 s.
citation: Card, S. K., Moran, T. P., & Newell, A. (1980). The keystroke-level model for user performance time with interactive systems. CACM, 23(7), 396–410.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Card, T. Moran & A. Newell
author: S. Card, T. Moran & A. Newell
title: Model Human Processor
statement: Human information processing can be approximated as perceptual, cognitive and motor processors with characteristic cycle times and memories with characteristic capacities and decay.
rationale: Explains why ~100 ms feels instantaneous and gives engineering estimates for reaction times.
audit_check: Are interface reactions within perceptual "instantaneous" range (~100 ms) for direct manipulation?
threshold: Perceptual ≈ 100 ms [50–200], cognitive ≈ 70 ms [25–170], motor ≈ 70 ms [30–100].
citation: Card, S. K., Moran, T. P., & Newell, A. (1983). The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction. Lawrence Erlbaum.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Card, T. Moran & A. Newell
author: S. Card, T. Moran & A. Newell
title: GOMS (Goals, Operators, Methods, Selection rules)
statement: Skilled behavior can be described as goals achieved through methods composed of operators, with selection rules for choosing methods.
rationale: Useful for analyzing and predicting expert efficiency and learning time of procedural interfaces.
audit_check: For expert workflows, are there efficient methods (shortcuts, bulk actions) and are selection rules simple?
citation: Card, Moran & Newell (1983); John, B. E. & Kieras, D. E. (1996). The GOMS family of user interface analysis techniques. ACM TOCHI, 3(4), 320–351.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. Hoober
title: Thumb zone / one-handed mobile use
statement: Observation of 1,333 people using phones found about 49% held the phone in one hand with thumb input; reach is easiest in the lower-middle area of the screen and hardest at the top corners.
rationale: Place frequent mobile actions within easy thumb reach (bottom area); avoid placing primary actions only in top corners on tall phones.
audit_check: On mobile, are frequent and primary actions reachable in the bottom/middle area of the screen?
citation: Hoober, S. (2013). How Do Users Really Hold Mobile Devices? UXmatters.

source_org: Parhi, Karlson & Bederson; MIT Touch Lab
author: Parhi, Karlson & Bederson; MIT Touch Lab
title: Finger and touch target size research
statement: Average adult finger pads are about 10–14 mm wide and fingertips 8–10 mm; one-handed thumb tapping error rates drop substantially for targets of about 9.2–9.6 mm and larger.
rationale: Make touch targets at least ~9 mm (≈ 44–48 px/pt/dp) with spacing between adjacent targets.
audit_check: Are touch targets at least 44×44 pt (iOS) / 48×48 dp (Android) or have equivalent spacing?
threshold: ≥ 9.6 mm (Parhi et al. 2006); 44 pt Apple HIG; 48 dp Material; WCAG 2.5.8 ≥ 24 CSS px; WCAG 2.5.5 ≥ 44 CSS px.
citation: Parhi, P., Karlson, A. K., & Bederson, B. B. (2006). Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices. MobileHCI '06, 203–210; Dandekar, K., Raju, B., & Srinivasan, M. (2003). 3-D finite-element models of human and monkey fingertips. J. Biomech. Eng.

source_org: R. B. Miller; S. Card et al.; J. Nielsen
author: R. B. Miller; S. Card et al.; J. Nielsen
title: Response time limits (0.1 s / 1 s / 10 s)
statement: About 0.1 s feels instantaneous; about 1 s keeps the user’s flow of thought uninterrupted though the delay is noticed; about 10 s is the limit for keeping attention on the dialogue.
rationale: Give immediate feedback within 0.1 s for direct manipulation; show progress indicators for anything over ~1 s; show percent-done progress and allow cancel for anything over ~10 s.
audit_check: Does every action give visible feedback within 100 ms? Are operations over 1 s accompanied by a loading indicator and over 10 s by a progress bar with cancel?
threshold: 0.1 s instantaneous; 1 s flow; 10 s attention.
citation: Miller, R. B. (1968). Response time in man-computer conversational transactions. AFIPS Fall Joint Computer Conference, 267–277; Card, S. K., Robertson, G. G., & Mackinlay, J. D. (1991). The information visualizer. CHI '91; Nielsen, J. (1993). Usability Engineering, ch. 5.

source_org: W. J. Doherty & A. J. Thadani
author: W. J. Doherty & A. J. Thadani
title: Doherty threshold
statement: Productivity rises sharply when system response time drops below about 400 ms, because users and computer interact at a pace where neither waits on the other.
rationale: Aim for interaction responses under 400 ms; use optimistic UI, skeletons and perceived-performance techniques when real work takes longer.
audit_check: Do routine interactions complete (or appear to complete) in under 400 ms?
citation: Doherty, W. J. & Thadani, A. J. (1982). The Economic Value of Rapid Response Time. IBM technical report GE20-0752-0.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Google Chrome team
title: RAIL performance model
statement: Response: process user input within 50 ms so visible response occurs within 100 ms; Animation: produce a frame in 10 ms (16 ms budget for 60 fps); Idle: work in ≤ 50 ms chunks; Load: deliver content and become interactive within ~5 s on mid-range mobile on slow networks (and subsequent loads within 2 s).
rationale: Gives engineering budgets aligned to perception limits.
audit_check: Do interactions respond within 100 ms and animations run at 60 fps without jank?
threshold: 100 ms response, 16 ms/frame, 50 ms idle chunks, ≤ 5 s load
citation: Google (2015). Measure performance with the RAIL model. web.dev.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Buell & M. Norton
title: Labor illusion
statement: People value a service more, and tolerate waiting better, when the system visibly shows the work being done on their behalf.
rationale: For unavoidable waits (search, quotes, AI generation), show meaningful progress steps. Do not add fake delays to manipulate perception.
audit_check: During long operations, does the UI show what is being done (meaningful steps) rather than a blank spinner?
citation: Buell, R. W. & Norton, M. I. (2011). The labor illusion: How operational transparency increases perceived value. Management Science, 57(9), 1564–1579.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Maister
title: Psychology of waiting lines
statement: Occupied time feels shorter than unoccupied time; uncertain and unexplained waits feel longer; anxious waits feel longer; unfair waits feel longer.
rationale: Tell users how long they will wait and why; keep them occupied with useful content; show queue position.
audit_check: Do waits show an estimated duration or position, and an explanation?
citation: Maister, D. H. (1985). The psychology of waiting lines. In Czepiel, Solomon & Surprenant (Eds.), The Service Encounter.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: C. Harrison, B. Amento, S. Kuznetsov & R. Bell
author: C. Harrison, B. Amento, S. Kuznetsov & R. Bell
title: Progress bar perception
statement: Progress bars that accelerate toward the end, or show backward-moving ribbing, are perceived as faster than linear ones, even when total duration is the same.
rationale: Avoid progress bars that stall near 100%; front-load uncertainty.
audit_check: Do progress indicators avoid stalling near completion?
citation: Harrison, C. et al. (2007). Rethinking the progress bar. UIST '07, 115–118.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: S. Iyengar & M. Lepper
title: Choice overload
statement: Offering too many options can reduce the likelihood of choosing at all and lower satisfaction with the choice (24 vs 6 jam varieties study). Effect size varies by context (Scheibehenne et al. 2010 meta-analysis found mean effect near zero but with moderators).
rationale: Curate options, provide defaults and recommendations, and offer filtering for large catalogs.
audit_check: Where users must choose (plans, products, settings), are options limited, compared clearly, and is a recommended option highlighted?
citation: Iyengar, S. S. & Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating. JPSP, 79(6), 995–1006; Scheibehenne, B., Greifeneder, R., & Todd, P. M. (2010). Can there ever be too many options? JCR, 37(3), 409–425.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: D. Kahneman & A. Tversky
title: Prospect theory & loss aversion
statement: People evaluate outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains (roughly 2×).
rationale: Framing in terms of what users would lose can motivate, but becomes manipulative when used to pressure (e.g., confirmshaming). Use honestly.
audit_check: Is loss framing used honestly and without pressure tactics?
citation: Kahneman, D. & Tversky, A. (1979). Prospect theory: An analysis of decision under risk. Econometrica, 47(2), 263–291.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Tversky & D. Kahneman
title: Framing effect
statement: Logically equivalent choices presented differently (e.g., "90% survive" vs "10% die") lead to different decisions.
rationale: Wording of consent, pricing and risk information shapes decisions; present information neutrally where users make consequential choices.
audit_check: Are consequential choices (consent, cancellations, risk) framed neutrally and clearly?
citation: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1981). The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice. Science, 211(4481), 453–458.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: A. Tversky & D. Kahneman
title: Anchoring
statement: People rely heavily on the first piece of information offered (the anchor) when making judgments.
rationale: The first price, number or option shown sets expectations; showing a fake "was" price is deceptive.
audit_check: Are reference prices and anchors genuine (not fabricated "was" prices)?
citation: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Johnson & D. Goldstein
title: Default effect
statement: People disproportionately stick with pre-selected defaults (organ donor consent rates differed hugely between opt-in and opt-out countries).
rationale: Set defaults that serve the user’s interest; never pre-select paid add-ons, marketing consent or data sharing (also prohibited under GDPR for consent).
audit_check: Are all defaults in the user’s interest? Are paid extras, marketing and data-sharing options unchecked by default?
citation: Johnson, E. J. & Goldstein, D. (2003). Do defaults save lives? Science, 302(5649), 1338–1339.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: J. Huber, J. Payne & C. Puto
author: J. Huber, J. Payne & C. Puto
title: Decoy effect (asymmetric dominance)
statement: Adding a third, clearly inferior option shifts preference toward the option that dominates it.
rationale: Common in pricing tables; ethical when it clarifies value, manipulative when the decoy exists only to steer.
audit_check: Does each pricing option exist for a genuine user segment, rather than only to steer choice?
citation: Huber, J., Payne, J. W., & Puto, C. (1982). Adding asymmetrically dominated alternatives. JCR, 9(1), 90–98.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: C. Hull; R. Kivetz, O. Urminsky & Y. Zheng
author: C. Hull; R. Kivetz, O. Urminsky & Y. Zheng
title: Goal-gradient effect
statement: Motivation and effort increase as people get closer to a goal.
rationale: Show progress and remaining steps; give a head start (endowed progress) where honest.
audit_check: Do multi-step flows show progress toward completion?
citation: Hull, C. L. (1932). The goal-gradient hypothesis and maze learning. Psychological Review, 39(1), 25–43; Kivetz, R., Urminsky, O., & Zheng, Y. (2006). The goal-gradient hypothesis resurrected. JMR, 43(1), 39–58.

author: J. Nunes & X. Drèze
title: Endowed progress effect
statement: People given artificial advancement toward a goal (e.g., a loyalty card with 2 of 10 stamps already filled) are more likely to complete it.
rationale: Starting progress bars from a non-zero state for already-completed steps (account created, email confirmed) increases completion.
audit_check: Do onboarding checklists reflect steps the user has already completed?
citation: Nunes, J. C. & Drèze, X. (2006). The endowed progress effect. JCR, 32(4), 504–512.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: D. Kahneman, B. Fredrickson, C. Schreiber & D. Redelmeier
author: D. Kahneman, B. Fredrickson, C. Schreiber & D. Redelmeier
title: Peak–end rule
statement: People judge an experience largely by how it felt at its most intense point and at its end, rather than by the average.
rationale: Design the emotional peaks (moments of success) and endings (confirmation pages, cancellation, offboarding) with care; a painful final step colors the whole experience.
audit_check: Are the final steps of key journeys (confirmation, cancellation, errors at the end) positive, clear and reassuring?
citation: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A., & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6), 401–405.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Yerkes & J. Dodson
title: Yerkes–Dodson law
statement: Performance increases with arousal up to an optimal point, then decreases; the optimum is lower for complex tasks.
rationale: Avoid adding stress (timers, alarming colors, urgency messaging) to complex tasks like forms, payments or medical decisions.
audit_check: Are complex tasks free of artificial pressure (countdown timers, alarming language)?
citation: Yerkes, R. M. & Dodson, J. D. (1908). The relation of strength of stimulus to rapidity of habit-formation. J. Comparative Neurology and Psychology, 18(5), 459–482.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: B. J. Fogg
title: Fogg Behavior Model (B = MAP)
statement: A behavior happens when Motivation, Ability and a Prompt converge at the same moment; if a behavior does not happen, at least one is missing.
rationale: Increase ability (make it simpler) before trying to increase motivation; prompt at the moment when motivation and ability are present.
audit_check: For the key conversion behavior, is the action simple enough (ability) and is there a clear prompt at the right moment?
citation: Fogg, B. J. (2009). A behavior model for persuasive design. Persuasive '09, Article 40.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: F. Davis
title: Technology Acceptance Model
statement: Intention to use a technology is driven mainly by perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use.
rationale: Adoption requires demonstrating usefulness early (value before effort) as well as reducing friction.
audit_check: Does the product communicate its usefulness before asking for effort (signup, setup)?
citation: Davis, F. D. (1989). Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and user acceptance of information technology. MIS Quarterly, 13(3), 319–340.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: V. Venkatesh, M. Morris, G. Davis & F. Davis
author: V. Venkatesh, M. Morris, G. Davis & F. Davis
title: Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT)
statement: Use intention is predicted by performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence and facilitating conditions, moderated by gender, age, experience and voluntariness.
rationale: Adoption also depends on social proof and on support/infrastructure, not only on the interface.
audit_check: Are support resources and social proof available for new users?
citation: Venkatesh, V. et al. (2003). User acceptance of information technology: Toward a unified view. MIS Quarterly, 27(3), 425–478.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Rogers
title: Diffusion of innovations
statement: Adoption spreads through innovators, early adopters, early majority, late majority and laggards; relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability drive adoption speed.
rationale: Trialability (free trials, demo modes) and observability (visible results) speed adoption; complexity slows it.
audit_check: Can users try the product before committing, and see results quickly?
citation: Rogers, E. M. (1962). Diffusion of Innovations. Free Press.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. Deci & R. Ryan
title: Self-determination theory
statement: Intrinsic motivation and well-being depend on satisfying three needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness.
rationale: Give users meaningful control and choices, help them feel competent (clear feedback, appropriate challenge), and support connection where relevant.
audit_check: Does the product give users control, build their sense of competence, and avoid controlling or coercive patterns?
citation: Deci, E. L. & Ryan, R. M. (1985). Intrinsic Motivation and Self-Determination in Human Behavior. Plenum.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Csikszentmihalyi
title: Flow
statement: Optimal experience occurs when challenge matches skill, goals are clear, and feedback is immediate; too much challenge causes anxiety, too little causes boredom.
rationale: Remove interruptions during focused work, give immediate feedback, and match difficulty to skill (progressive complexity).
audit_check: During focused tasks, are interruptions (modals, prompts, notifications) avoided?
citation: Csikszentmihalyi, M. (1990). Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience. Harper & Row.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: K. Stanovich & R. West; D. Kahneman
author: K. Stanovich & R. West; D. Kahneman
title: Dual-process theory (System 1 / System 2)
statement: Thinking runs on a fast, automatic, intuitive system and a slow, effortful, deliberate system; most interface use relies on the fast system.
rationale: Design for fast intuitive use (conventions, clear signifiers) and deliberately slow users down only where consequences are serious (confirmation of irreversible actions).
audit_check: Are routine tasks executable on autopilot, and are high-stakes, irreversible actions deliberately slowed (review step, explicit confirmation)?
citation: Stanovich, K. E. & West, R. F. (2000). Individual differences in reasoning. BBS, 23(5), 645–665; Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Cialdini
title: Cialdini's principles of influence
statement: Reciprocity, commitment & consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity, and (2016) unity drive compliance.
rationale: These levers are powerful and must be used truthfully: fake scarcity, fake social proof and fake authority are deceptive patterns and may be illegal.
audit_check: Are scarcity, social proof, and authority claims truthful and verifiable?
citation: Cialdini, R. B. (1984). Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion; Cialdini (2016). Pre-Suasion.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Thaler & C. Sunstein
title: Nudge / choice architecture
statement: How choices are presented (defaults, ordering, framing, salience) predictably influences decisions without restricting options; nudges should be transparent and easy to opt out of.
rationale: Use choice architecture to help users act in their own interest (e.g., saving), and avoid "sludge" that makes beneficial actions harder.
audit_check: Does the choice architecture help users act in their own interest, with easy opt-out? Is there sludge making beneficial actions (cancel, opt-out, claim) harder than harmful ones?
citation: Thaler, R. H. & Sunstein, C. R. (2008). Nudge. Yale University Press; Sunstein, C. (2020). Sludge audits. Behavioural Public Policy.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Behavioural Insights Team
title: EAST framework
statement: To encourage a behavior, make it Easy, Attractive, Social and Timely.
rationale: Practical checklist for designing interventions in services.
audit_check: Is the desired behavior easy (defaults, fewer steps), attractive (salient, rewarding), social (norms), and timely (prompted at the right moment)?
citation: Behavioural Insights Team (2014). EAST: Four simple ways to apply behavioural insights.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: S. Michie, M. van Stralen & R. West
author: S. Michie, M. van Stralen & R. West
title: COM-B model / Behaviour Change Wheel
statement: Behavior results from Capability, Opportunity and Motivation interacting.
rationale: Diagnose why users do not perform a behavior before designing interventions.
audit_check: Has the team diagnosed whether non-completion is due to capability, opportunity or motivation?
citation: Michie, S., van Stralen, M. M., & West, R. (2011). The behaviour change wheel. Implementation Science, 6, 42.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: N. Eyal
title: Hook model
statement: Habit-forming products cycle users through trigger → action → variable reward → investment.
rationale: Understand it to recognize compulsive loops; variable rewards and infinite feeds can harm well-being. Audit for manipulative engagement loops.
audit_check: Do engagement loops serve the user’s goals, and can users easily stop (no infinite autoplay without control, clear stopping cues)?
citation: Eyal, N. (2014). Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: M. Norton, D. Mochon & D. Ariely
author: M. Norton, D. Mochon & D. Ariely
title: IKEA effect
statement: People place disproportionately high value on things they partially created themselves.
rationale: Light customization and setup investment can increase attachment; but required effort should not become a lock-in tactic.
audit_check: Is user investment (customization, content) portable and not used as lock-in?
citation: Norton, M. I., Mochon, D., & Ariely, D. (2012). The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love. JCP, 22(3), 453–460.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: R. Zajonc
title: Mere-exposure effect
statement: People develop a preference for things merely because they are familiar with them.
rationale: Familiar conventions feel better and are trusted more; radical redesigns often meet initial resistance regardless of quality.
audit_check: Does the interface use familiar conventions where possible?
citation: Zajonc, R. B. (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. JPSP, 9(2, Pt.2), 1–27.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Nielsen
title: Jakob's law
statement: Users spend most of their time on other sites, so they prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know.
rationale: Follow established conventions for navigation, forms, carts, search and controls; innovate where it adds real value.
audit_check: Does the interface follow platform and industry conventions (logo top-left links home, cart top-right, standard form controls)?
citation: Nielsen, J. (2000). End of Web Design. Alertbox, July 23, 2000.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: L. Tesler
title: Tesler's law (law of conservation of complexity)
statement: Every application has an inherent amount of complexity that cannot be removed; it can only be shifted between the system and the user.
rationale: The system (and its designers/developers) should absorb complexity rather than pushing it onto users (e.g., auto-detect card type, parse addresses, infer time zones).
audit_check: Is complexity that the system could handle (formatting, inference, defaults) being pushed onto the user?
citation: Saffer, D. (2009). Designing for Interaction (interview with Larry Tesler); originally articulated at Xerox PARC in the mid-1980s.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: J. Postel
title: Postel's law (robustness principle)
statement: Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others.
rationale: Accept user input in many formats (spaces in phone numbers, dashes in card numbers, varied date formats) and normalize it; output consistent, clean formats.
audit_check: Do form fields accept common variations (spaces, dashes, capitalization, leading/trailing whitespace) instead of rejecting them?
citation: Postel, J. (1980). RFC 760: DoD Standard Internet Protocol; restated in RFC 793 (1981).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: William of Ockham
title: Occam's razor
statement: Among competing hypotheses or solutions that work equally well, the one with the fewest assumptions or elements should be selected.
rationale: Remove any element that does not contribute to the user’s goal.
audit_check: Can any element be removed without hurting the user’s ability to complete their task?
citation: Principle predating the period; widely applied in design.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: V. Pareto; J. Juran
title: Pareto principle (80/20 rule)
statement: Roughly 80% of effects come from 20% of causes.
rationale: A small subset of features and tasks accounts for most use; optimize the top tasks first and avoid letting rare tasks clutter the main interface.
audit_check: Are the most frequent tasks the most prominent and efficient?
citation: Juran, J. M. (1951). Quality Control Handbook (popularized "vital few").
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: C. N. Parkinson
title: Parkinson's law
statement: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
rationale: Short, well-defined tasks (with sensible estimates of time required) feel achievable; autofill and defaults reduce time-to-complete.
audit_check: Do forms and tasks indicate expected time and avoid unnecessary steps?
citation: Parkinson, C. N. (1955). Parkinson's law. The Economist, November 19, 1955.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: M. Conway
title: Conway's law
statement: Organizations design systems that mirror their own communication structures.
rationale: Navigation and products often reflect org charts rather than user tasks; audit IA for organization-centric labels and silos.
audit_check: Is the navigation organized around user tasks rather than internal departments or product teams?
citation: Conway, M. E. (1968). How do committees invent? Datamation, 14(4), 28–31.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: C. Goodhart
title: Goodhart's law
statement: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.
rationale: Optimizing a single UX metric (time on site, clicks, NPS) leads to gaming and worse experiences; use balanced metrics (e.g., HEART) and qualitative evidence.
audit_check: Are success metrics balanced so that optimizing one does not harm users (e.g., engagement vs. task success)?
citation: Goodhart, C. (1975). Problems of monetary management: The U.K. experience; Strathern, M. (1997) phrasing.
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: E. A. Murphy Jr.
title: Murphy's law
statement: Anything that can go wrong will go wrong.
rationale: Design every flow for error states, edge cases, empty states, offline states and misuse.
audit_check: Have error, empty, loading, offline and edge-case states been designed for every key screen?
citation: Attributed to Edward A. Murphy Jr., Edwards Air Force Base (1949).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Attributed to K. Johnson
title: KISS (keep it simple)
statement: Most systems work best if they are kept simple rather than made complicated.
rationale: Simplicity should be a design goal; unnecessary complexity should be avoided.
audit_check: Is the solution the simplest one that meets user needs?
citation: Attributed to Kelly Johnson, Lockheed Skunk Works (c. 1960).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

author: Programming & UI design folklore
title: Principle of least astonishment (POLA)
statement: A component of a system should behave in the way most users expect it to behave; it should not astonish or surprise users.
rationale: If a design surprises users, change the design, not the users.
audit_check: Does any control behave differently from what its appearance and label suggest?
citation: Commonly cited in PL/I and UI literature from the early 1970s (e.g., James, 1987, The Tao of Programming).
license: Original summary written for this knowledge base (free to use); cite the original source

source_org: M. Kurosu & K. Kashimura; N. Tractinsky
author: M. Kurosu & K. Kashimura; N. Tractinsky
title: Aesthetic–usability effect
statement: Users perceive more aesthetically pleasing designs as easier to use, and are more tolerant of minor usability issues in them.
rationale: Visual polish improves perceived usability and trust, but can mask real usability problems in testing; measure task performance, not just opinions.
audit_check: Is visual quality consistent and professional? In testing, are performance metrics used alongside satisfaction ratings?
citation: Kurosu, M. & Kashimura, K. (1995). Apparent usability vs. inherent usability. CHI '95 Conference Companion, 292–293; Tractinsky, N. (1997). Aesthetics and apparent usability. CHI '97.

source_org: N. Tractinsky, A. Katz & D. Ikar
author: N. Tractinsky, A. Katz & D. Ikar
title: What is beautiful is usable
statement: Perceived aesthetics of an interface correlated strongly with perceived usability both before and after use, even when actual usability was manipulated.
rationale: First impressions of visual design shape credibility and willingness to continue.
audit_check: Does the first view look credible and well-crafted?
citation: Tractinsky, N., Katz, A. S., & Ikar, D. (2000). What is beautiful is usable. Interacting with Computers, 13(2), 127–145.

source_org: G. Lindgaard, G. Fernandes, C. Dudek & J. Brown
author: G. Lindgaard, G. Fernandes, C. Dudek & J. Brown
title: First impressions in 50 milliseconds
statement: People form stable judgments of a web page’s visual appeal within about 50 ms of exposure.
rationale: Above-the-fold visual quality and clarity heavily influence whether users stay.
audit_check: Does the initial viewport communicate quality and purpose at a glance?
citation: Lindgaard, G. et al. (2006). Attention web designers: You have 50 milliseconds to make a good first impression! BIT, 25(2), 115–126.

source_org: K. Reinecke et al.; A. Tuch et al.
author: K. Reinecke et al.; A. Tuch et al.
title: Visual complexity and prototypicality
statement: Websites with low visual complexity and high prototypicality (looking like a typical site of their category) are judged most appealing in first impressions.
rationale: Keep visual complexity low and follow category conventions for landing pages.
audit_check: Is the visual complexity of key pages low, and does the page look like a typical member of its category?
citation: Tuch, A. N. et al. (2012). The role of visual complexity and prototypicality regarding first impression of websites. IJHCS, 70(11), 794–811; Reinecke, K. et al. (2013). Predicting users' first impressions of website aesthetics. CHI '13.
